title: Disclaimer Level Three: the most convoluted way to read one sentence
subtitle: SATIRE. Every gate below is a joke, except that you can really bark at gate 3. The recording stays in your browser and is never sent to us.
summary: In English defamation law, what you meant does not decide what you said. The ordinary reasonable reader decides, reading the whole publication, disclaimers included. So every disclaimer is more text to be read, and a pile of them can start to suggest exactly what it denies. This page takes that problem to its logical end: seven gates, five captchas, a 72-hour freezer and an exam, all standing between you and one sentence. The last section is not satire. It sets out what actually works: writing so the meaning is clear the first time.
scope: England and Wales · Satire about how the law reads disclaimers, built on the meaning test as stated by the courts, followed by a plain section on what protects a writer. It names no person and makes no allegation about anyone.
status_note: SATIRE, labelled as such, except the section headed “What actually works (not satire)” and the notes. Most gates do not exist: there is no timer, freezer or exam. Gate 3 works: if you press Bark and allow it, your browser records up to five seconds, which you can play back or save to your own device. The page has no code that uploads or stores anything, and the word-of-honour checklist never leaves the page. The legal statements are taken from the judgments and legislation cited. This is commentary and public education, not legal advice.

sections.title: The problem
sections.intro: Not satire yet. This is the rule the rest of the page makes fun of.

entries.kind: Court of Appeal test, as quoted by the High Court
entries.title: The reader decides, reading everything

paragraphs.text: In English defamation law, what a publication means is decided by the hypothetical ordinary reasonable reader, who is “not naïve but … not unduly suspicious”, “can read between the lines” and “can read in an implication more readily than a lawyer”. Two of the rules in the standard summary do the damage here: “The intention of the publisher is irrelevant” and “The article must be read as a whole, and any ‘bane and antidote’ taken together.” A disclaimer is part of the whole. It helps only if it actually changes what that reader understands.

sources.locator: para 57, quoting Jeynes: the meaning test

paragraphs.text: So every disclaimer is itself read. “I am not suggesting anything” is a sentence, and sentences carry implications. Pile on enough of them and the pile starts to suggest something. The author cannot prove what they do not mean, because each denial is more text for the reasonable reader to interpret.

sources.locator: para 57, quoting Jeynes: the meaning test

entries.kind: High Court judgment quoting the Court of Appeal
entries.title: Why “level three”

paragraphs.text: The courts grade implied allegations in three “Chase levels”, after Chase v News Group Newspapers (2002): the person is guilty; there are reasonable grounds to suspect they are; there are grounds to investigate whether they are. Level three is the lightest, and it can still be defamatory and still has to be defended. Hence the title.

paragraphs.text: Having barked, wiggled, rotated, waited three days and passed an exam, you are no longer an ordinary reader. You are now a highly unusual one, and the law was never asking about you: the hypothetical reader “is taken to be representative of those who would read the publication in question”.

sections.title: What actually works (not satire)
sections.intro: The way out of the disclaimer spiral is not more disclaimers. It is writing so the meaning is clear the first time.

entries.title: Aim satire at systems, not named people

paragraphs.text: Disclaimer culture, incentives and the reasonable-reader test are fair targets. A named person with an implied factual charge is where the risk returns, whatever the label says. Seven words and a stage direction were enough in McAlpine v Bercow.

entries.title: Separate fact, opinion and hypothesis visibly

paragraphs.text: Label each claim for what it is. Our Frameworks of truth page proposes five provenance labels for disputed claims: asserted, signed, supported, checked and found.

The honest-opinion defence protects a statement of opinion that indicates, in general or specific terms, the basis of the opinion, where an honest person could have held it on facts that existed at the time. The public-interest defence protects a statement on a matter of public interest that the publisher reasonably believed it was in the public interest to publish. Neither protects a hint dressed up as a hypothetical.

Defamation is civil. Separately, it is a criminal offence to send a message conveying information you know to be false, intending it to cause non-trivial psychological or physical harm to a likely audience, without reasonable excuse. Sending a threat of death or serious harm, intending or being reckless as to whether someone fears it will be carried out, is another offence. Section 180 contains exemptions we have not analysed here.

Your own description of your conduct does not decide its legal character. Phil Ivey sincerely believed edge-sorting was not cheating; the Supreme Court held that it was. That applies to the word “satire” too: a satire label is a label.

We read McAlpine v Bercow and Depp v News Group Newspapers from the National Archives, and sections 3 and 4 of the Defamation Act 2013 and sections 179 and 181 of the Online Safety Act 2023 from legislation.gov.uk, on 30 October and 5 November 2026. Charleston v News Group Newspapers [1995] 2 AC 65, the House of Lords case usually cited for reading “bane and antidote” together, and Chase v News Group Newspapers [2002] EWCA Civ 1772 could not be opened. Both principles are cited through their quotation in later judgments.

paragraphs.text: It is not a disclaimer for any other page, and it is not linked to any page as one. It does not discuss every defence, the serious-harm test in section 1, or the law of Scotland and Northern Ireland. This is commentary, not legal advice.
